transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Redwood SA); Sara Lin (CTO, AstraNova), Dev Patel (Eng Lead), Kofi Mensah (SRE), Lena Fischer (Security)

Summary:
- AstraNova is evaluating dedicated/reserved GPUs vs hosted for a latency-sensitive inference product (gen+chat + embeddings). They need isolation, burst handling for marketing spikes, and predictable unit economics.
- Primary constraints: EU data residency, SOC2 + KMS, latency p95 ~150-250ms for short generation (~64 tokens) but can accept longer for longer sequences.
- Next steps: pricing, short perf bench, share traffic histogram and compliance checklist.

Topics: reservations vs warm pools; tenant isolation and pre-warm; burst tolerance and eviction/fallback; private/VPC path; SLOs, quantization and cost tradeoffs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everybody thanks for joining, can we do quick intros then jump into how you're thinking about dedicated vs hosted?
[00:12] Sara (CTO): Sure. I'm Sara, CTO. We run a multimodal assistant and we expect heavy marketing spikes around product announcements, maybe 3x baseline for short windows. Latency is a hard bar for UX.
[00:25] Dev (Eng Lead): Dev here—main ask is isolation for IP and also predictable tail latency. We currently self-host a mix but we want to evaluate Redwood for either reserved capacity or private deployment.
[00:35] Maya: Great. Diego from SE will cover performance and config questions. Diego, want to frame what people usually ask?
[00:41] Diego (SE): Yep. Two vectors: steady throughput (monthly commits) and burst. For reserved capacity we size by concurrent requests or tokens/sec. For bursts we have warm-pool prewarmed nodes and a burst guardrail. Quick question for AstraNova: what's your 95th latency SLO target for short responses?
[00:58] Sara: We're aiming for p95 under 250ms for 64-token replies, ideally 150ms but not sure how realistic that is for some of your open models.
[01:08] Diego: That's doable in many cases depending on model size, quantization, and batching. If you want deterministic p95 you lean into dedicated with pinned models and prewarmed cores; warm pool helps absorb short spikes.
[01:20] Kofi (SRE): How does eviction work? Say we reserve N GPUs but sudden surge beyond policy—will other tenants preempt? We need strict tenant fencing for regulatory reasons.
[01:33] Priya (SA): Good question. Reserved capacity gives you isolated pools (no noisy neighbor), eviction only happens if you configure burst to cross into shared capacity. We can set hard isolation: no shared fallback, or a soft fallback to a smaller quantized variant if you accept quality drop.
[01:49] Dev: So fallback to a quantized variant—what are the typical quality regressions you'd expect? Any examples?
[01:55] Diego: For 4-bit quant vs fp16, you might see occasional tokenization differences and subtle semantic shifts. We run eval sets to quantify delta and can surface regression alerts in Redwood Optimize.
[02:08] Lena (Security): On encryption—does Redwood support customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for model artifacts and logs? Also we need audit logs and SSO (SAML).
[02:17] Maya: Yes to KMS integration in Private and Dedicated; hosted has envelope encryption with managed KMS but can integrate external keys for enterprise plans. Audit logs and SAML SSO are standard on enterprise tiers. We'll share the SOC2 cert and a short compliance pack.
[02:30] Sara: Good. We also need EU residency — any region constraints?
[02:34] Priya: We have eu-west-1 and eu-central regions for hosted and dedicated placement. For Private you can run in your VPC in EU or on-prem.
[02:41] Dev: Let's get more granular on sizing. Right now our steady traffic is roughly 200 rps baseline for short queries with avg seq len 45 tokens; spikes push to 600rps for 10-20 minute windows. How would you recommend sizing reserved GPUs?
[02:55] Diego: A rough heuristic: estimate tokens/sec = rps * avg_seq. For your baseline 200rps * 45 = 9k tokens/sec. On an A100-class GPU at fp16 with optimized kernels you might get ~30-60k tokens/sec depending on model; but exacts vary. For safety, we model two scenarios: conservative (assume 25k toks/s per GPU) or optimistic (50k). So baseline could be 1 GPU with headroom, but spikes to 600rps may need warm pool + 1-2 burst nodes.
[03:25] Dev: We run a Llama2-13B-ish variant with custom fine-tune; also KV cache tends to bloat for longer dialogues.
[03:32] Diego: KV cache changes memory footprint—if you keep long context we recommend larger memory nodes or sharded KV across GPUs. For reserved, you can pick node types with more memory or enable pinned KV.
[03:42] Kofi: What about start-up time for warm pool? We need sub-60s for providing new capacity during spike.
[03:48] Priya: Warm pools are pre-warmed runtimes; typical prewarm time for model load is 10-40s depending on model and quantization; we keep hot pools to keep them <30s. There's warm-pool stickiness so hot nodes remain hot for a window to avoid cold starts.
[03:59] Sara: If we go private (VPC), can we still use Redwood's warm pools or do we need to manage that ourselves?
[04:04] Maya: In Private deployment you get the same runtime but managed by customer; we offer an optional managed warm-pool orchestrator for Private customers as an add-on.
[04:12] Dev: Pricing question—if we reserve N GPUs plus burst, is burst billed differently? Is it per-minute?
[04:20] Maya: Reserved capacity is monthly commitment; burst usage beyond commit is billed at an overage rate per GPU-hour or per-token depending on agreement. We can model both approaches; for short bursts sometimes per-minute granularity is better. We'll include both options in the pricing sheet.
[04:33] Kofi: SLA—what uptime and latency SLOs do you provide for dedicated?
[04:37] Priya: SLA for Dedicated typically covers availability (e.g., 99.9% compute availability) and regional redundancy can be added. For latency SLOs we work with customers to define p95 targets; guarantees depend on topology and reserved sizing.
[04:49] Dev: Any constraints around custom kernels or our in-house ops? We might want to bring our own runtime patches.
[04:54] Diego: For hosted we don't accept arbitrary customer kernels for security. For Dedicated or Private there is more flexibility: Dedicated (managed) allows limited extensions via vetted images; Private (customer-managed) gives you full control but we lose some telemetry. We'll document the tradeoffs.
[05:07] Sara: For our compliance team—what's the data retention for logs and how easy is it to pull audit trails?
[05:12] Maya: Logs retention is configurable for enterprise. Audit trails can be exported via API and we support SIEM forwarding. We'll include a sample retention policy and the audit export API in the pack.
[05:21] Dev: Could we set different routing policies per route? For example, low-latency user-facing route pinned to dedicated, long-running batch route to cheaper hosted variants?
[05:29] Priya: Yes—smart routing allows per-route policies. You can pin a route to a dedicated pool and have fallback to hosted or a quantized cheaper model for non-critical routes.
[05:36] Sara: We need to understand failure modes: if dedicated pool saturates in a global event, what's Redwood's recommended fallback?
[05:43] Diego: Recommended: define a chain: primary dedicated -> secondary dedicated in other region (if enabled) -> hosted compatible variant with throttling and degraded quality warning. Also set circuit-breakers and a gradual shedding policy. We can simulate in an SRE runbook.
[05:55] Dev: Are there per-tenant guardrails to prevent single team from blasting the pool?
[06:00] Priya: Yes, token-level quotas, rate limits and per-token cost dashboards; you can set burst credits per tenant. For multi-team orgs we enforce per-API-key quotas and have governance dashboards.
[06:12] Kofi: Onboarding timeline—what's realistic for reserved capacity? We might want a pilot asap for Black Friday testing.
[06:18] Maya: Typical pilot is 2-4 weeks: initial config + 1-2 perf runs + small reserved commit. Full rollouts take longer depending on procurement. If you want a high-confidence spike test before Black Friday we'd recommend starting pilot by mid-November.
[06:31] Sara: Procurement constraints: we have limits on long-term financial commitments; what flexibility for short term reserve or pilot credit?
[06:38] Maya: We can do a time-limited pilot and then convert to reserved with a pro-rated commit. Also, there's reserved trial credits for qualifying pilots. We'll propose options.
[06:48] Dev: Regarding metrics we will send you our traffic histograms—percentiles for seq len and request arrival distribution—can that drive a more accurate sizing?
[06:56] Diego: Absolutely. The more granular the histogram (per-minute over sample days) the better our model and kernel selection suggestions. We'll run a small capacity model to simulate.
[07:05] Lena: Security detail—does Redwood provide HSM-level key wrapping or just KMS? We have an HSM requirement for some keys.
[07:11] Priya: We support customer-managed HSM integration for Private and Dedicated enterprise tiers. We'll add the HSM integration doc.
[07:19] Sara: One more on regional failover: if eu-west fails, can we divert to eu-central without violating data residency for certain PII routes?
[07:27] Maya: You can configure per-route residency policies to block cross-region fallback for sensitive routes. For non-sensitive routes you can allow cross-region fallback.
[07:36] Dev: Can we try a quick hypothetical sizing: say baseline 200rps, spike 600rps, avg seq 45, model is ~13B. What would a recommendation look like?
[07:45] Diego: We'll run numbers but quick answer: 2 reserved GPUs with a 1-GPU warm pool and 1-2 burst nodes in shared burst pool if you accept shared fallback; otherwise 3 dedicated GPUs to cover spikes with headroom. We'll provide a spreadsheet with conservative/optimistic columns.
[07:58] Sara: Any tooling to detect quality regressions when falling back to quantized variants?
[08:03] Maya: Redwood Optimize includes evaluation hooks that can run your test prompts and flag regressions on rollout and fallback. We'll propose an eval set run during pilot.
[08:14] Kofi: For chaos tests—do you provide a failover playbook and runbook templates?
[08:18] Priya: Yes, we have SRE playbooks and a sample chaos test harness; we can share the doc and run a tabletop if you'd like.
[08:27] Dev: Great. Logistics—who on your side will own the pilot?
[08:31] Maya: I'll own commercial and pilot SOW; Diego will run the perf bench; Priya will be the touchpoint for architecture.
[08:38] Sara: Perfect. Let's align on timeline: we'll aim to send traffic histograms by 11/6, expect your pricing by 11/7, and want the perf bench week of 11/10.
[08:48] Maya: Yep that aligns.
[08:52] (brief cross-talk, small audio glitch)
[09:05] Diego: One technical note—if your model uses a custom tokenizer or special ops, bring the containerized artifact for the bench; that short-circuits a lot of surprises.
[09:16] Dev: We'll do that. Also, question about model pinning and rollbacks. If we push a new model that regresses, can you auto-fallback to previous pinned version?
[09:25] Priya: Yes we support canary and automatic rollback policies based on latency/quality regressions. You can pin model versions per route.
[09:33] Sara: Great. That covers most of our questions.
[09:36] Maya: Quick recap then next steps — we'll send pricing + pilot SOW, SE will run perf bench once you share the model and traffic histogram, and security will get compliance pack. Any blockers?
[09:47] Lena: No blockers; just need SOC2, HSM detail, and SAML flow diagram.
[09:52] Maya: We'll include those in the pack. Thanks everyone.
[09:55] End meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: auto-transcription had a few mis-typed product names; speakers correctly identified most of the time but sometimes overlapped; we've kept filler words and short interruptions to preserve authenticity.
